books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.7 A: In the 1820s, most states reduced or removed property qualifications for voting, so most free white males could vote. The push was strongest in the newly admitted states of the West. Ohio, admitted in 1803, led the way, letting any voter hold public office. Between 1816 and 1821, six new states also wrote broader voting rules into their constitutions. Land was cheaper and more widely available in the West, so fewer men there were landless. In the 1820s, older states felt pressure from popular movements to follow, and most reduced property qualifications, though many still required voters to be taxpayers. Historians estimate that about 90 percent of adult white men could vote by 1840.
stimulus.source_note: Secondary text: paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.7 A. Paraphrased, not quoted.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Which development best explains why western states moved first to expand voting rights?

options.text: Western states had older constitutions than the Atlantic states
options.misconception: Their constitutions were newer, written when the states were admitted, not older.

options.text: Western states depended on enslaved labor more than the East did
options.misconception: The passage ties the change to cheap land, not to slavery.

options.text: Western states were pressured by the federal government to change
options.misconception: The pressure came from popular movements and western example, not from Washington.

options.text: Cheap, widely available land meant fewer western men were landless

rationales.A: The western constitutions were new, written at admission, which is why they could be broader.
rationales.B: The passage ties the western lead to cheap land, not to slavery.
rationales.C: The pressure came from popular movements, not from the federal government.
rationales.D: With land cheap and widely available, fewer western men were landless, so a property rule shut out fewer voters and was easier to drop.
rationales.general:
1. Link land to voting. A property rule bars landless men, so where land is cheap, the rule bites fewer people.
2. Apply it to the West. Land was cheaper and more widely available there than in the original thirteen states.
3. Add the timing. Ohio led in 1803 and six new states followed between 1816 and 1821, before the older states moved.
Background: In the East, land was scarcer and dearer, so more men were landless and the property rule mattered more.
Remember: voting rules follow who owns land, so ask about land first.
